q: What is OpenStack and which core services make up a typical private cloud?
a: OpenStack is an open-source cloud operating system that turns a pool of servers, storage and network gear into a self-service infrastructure-as-a-service platform. You consume it through APIs, a CLI and the Horizon dashboard. The core services I always name are Keystone for identity, Nova for compute, Neutron for networking, Glance for images, Cinder for block storage, Placement for resource inventory, and Horizon for the UI. Swift gives object storage, Heat does orchestration, Octavia handles load balancing, and Ironic manages bare metal. Each service exposes a REST API, keeps state in a shared database, and talks to its own agents over a message queue, usually RabbitMQ. In an interview I stress that OpenStack is a set of loosely coupled projects, so you pick the ones you need. A small cloud might run only Keystone, Nova, Neutron, Glance and Cinder.
f: Which services are optional?
How do services authenticate to each other?
p: OpenStack is a set of loosely coupled services exposing REST APIs. The essentials are Keystone (identity), Nova (compute), Neutron (network), Glance (images), Cinder (block storage) and Placement (inventory), with Horizon as the UI.
tip: Say that services share a database and a message bus, then name the minimum viable set.

q: Describe the OpenStack control-plane architecture: API, database, message queue and agents.
a: Every OpenStack service follows a similar shape. An API process receives REST calls and validates the token with Keystone. It writes the desired state to a MariaDB or MySQL database, usually a Galera cluster. For long-running work it casts or calls a message over RabbitMQ using oslo.messaging. Worker daemons, such as nova-conductor, nova-scheduler and nova-compute, or neutron agents, pick up those messages and do the real work on hosts. Results flow back through the queue or the database. This is why RabbitMQ and the database are the two shared dependencies you protect most carefully. If the queue backs up, API calls succeed but nothing happens. If the database is slow, everything slows down. Behind a load balancer such as HAProxy, you run several copies of every API and conductor, which gives horizontal scale and high availability on the controller nodes.
f: Why is nova-conductor needed?
What breaks first when RabbitMQ is unhealthy?
p: API services validate tokens, persist state in Galera, and hand work to workers through RabbitMQ (oslo.messaging). The database and the queue are the shared dependencies to protect.
tip: Explain the failure mode: API accepts the request but no worker consumes it.

q: Walk through what happens, step by step, when a user runs openstack server create.
a: The client first gets a token from Keystone, then calls the Nova API with the flavor, image and network. Nova validates the request, checks quota, and writes an instance record in the database in the building state. The nova-scheduler asks the Placement service for candidate resource providers that have enough vCPU, RAM and disk, then applies filters and weights to choose a host. The conductor sends the build request to nova-compute on that host over the message queue. Compute asks Glance for the image, asks Neutron to create and bind a port, and asks Cinder if there is a volume. Libvirt then defines and starts the guest on KVM. Neutron wires the port with OVS or OVN and DHCP delivers the address. When the guest is running, Nova marks the instance ACTIVE. Knowing this order is how you localise a failure fast.
f: Where does the scheduler get its data?
At which step does a no valid host error appear?
p: Keystone token, Nova API and quota, scheduler with Placement, conductor to compute, then Glance image, Neutron port and Cinder volume, and finally libvirt starts the guest.
cmds: openstack server create --flavor m1.small --image ubuntu-22.04 --network private --key-name mykey web1
openstack server show web1 -c status -c fault
tip: Narrate it in order, then say which log you would open at each step.

q: OpenStack versus VMware vSphere versus Kubernetes: how do you position each?
a: They solve different layers. VMware vSphere is a polished, commercially supported virtualisation stack with strong tooling and licensing cost. OpenStack is an open-source infrastructure API layer that gives you multi-tenant compute, network and storage as a service, with no per-socket licence but real operational effort. Kubernetes orchestrates containers and assumes it already has machines and networks underneath. They are often combined: Kubernetes runs on top of OpenStack VMs or bare metal, using Cinder volumes and Octavia load balancers. I choose OpenStack when an organisation wants a private cloud with self-service, tenant isolation, open APIs, and freedom from licence lock-in, and has a team to run it. I pick VMware when operational simplicity and vendor support outweigh cost. I pick plain Kubernetes when the workloads are all containers and there is no need to offer VMs.
f: When would you not run OpenStack?
How does Kubernetes consume OpenStack?
p: vSphere is a supported virtualisation product, OpenStack is an open IaaS API layer, and Kubernetes orchestrates containers on top of either. They are complementary, not exclusive.
tip: Frame it as layers, not rivals, and be honest about the operational cost of running OpenStack.

q: Explain regions, availability zones, host aggregates and cells. How do they differ?
a: These are four different ways to partition a cloud. A region is a complete deployment with its own API endpoints, usually in a separate site, sharing only Keystone if you choose. An availability zone is a user-visible failure domain inside a region, such as a rack or power zone, which users select to spread instances. A host aggregate is an operator-only grouping of compute hosts with metadata, used for things like GPU hosts, SSD hosts or licence-bound hosts, and tied to flavors through scheduler filters. Cells are a Nova scaling mechanism: each cell has its own database and message queue for its computes, and a top-level API database routes to them. So AZs are for tenants, aggregates are for operators, cells are for scale, and regions are for geography. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: Can a host be in several aggregates?
Why do cells reduce load on RabbitMQ?
p: Region: a whole deployment. AZ: tenant-visible failure domain. Aggregate: operator grouping with metadata. Cell: scaling shard with its own DB and queue.
tip: Use the one-line summary: AZs for tenants, aggregates for operators, cells for scale.

q: What is the Placement service and why was it split out of Nova?
a: Placement is a small service that tracks inventory and usage of resources. A resource provider, such as a compute node, reports inventories of VCPU, MEMORY_MB and DISK_GB. Consumers, such as instances, claim allocations against those providers. Placement also supports traits, which are qualitative tags like HW_CPU_X86_AVX2 or CUSTOM_GPU, and aggregates and nested providers for things like NUMA nodes and GPUs. Nova used to compute free capacity itself in the scheduler and that was slow and racy. Splitting it out gave a generic, fast, queryable inventory service that Nova, Cyborg and Neutron can all use, for example for bandwidth-aware scheduling. The scheduler now asks Placement for allocation candidates first, then applies filters. When capacity looks wrong, I compare the Placement allocations with what Nova thinks is running, because drift between them causes phantom no valid host errors.
f: What are traits used for?
How do you fix stale allocations?
p: Placement stores resource providers, inventories, allocations and traits. Nova asks it for allocation candidates before running its filters, which is faster and less racy than the old in-scheduler accounting.
tip: Mention allocation drift as the thing you actually debug in production.

q: How does the Nova scheduler pick a host? Explain filters and weighers.
a: Scheduling is a two-stage funnel. First, Placement returns allocation candidates that have enough raw resources. Second, the scheduler runs an ordered list of filters, each of which can reject a host. Common ones are AvailabilityZoneFilter, ComputeFilter, ImagePropertiesFilter, ServerGroupAntiAffinityFilter, NUMATopologyFilter and AggregateInstanceExtraSpecsFilter. Hosts that survive are then ranked by weighers, for example RAMWeigher, which by default spreads load onto the host with most free RAM, or a custom weigher that packs instead. The highest weight wins, with some randomness among the top hosts to avoid stampedes. When you see no valid host was found, the useful move is to read the scheduler log, which prints how many hosts each filter removed, and that tells you whether the issue is capacity, a trait, an aggregate or an affinity rule. I would also mention the main failure mode and how I would detect it early, since operations experience shows in how you talk about what goes wrong.
f: Spread versus pack: how do you change it?
How do you debug no valid host?
p: Placement narrows candidates by raw capacity, filters reject hosts on policy, and weighers rank the remainder. The scheduler log shows how many hosts each filter removed.
tip: Say you debug no valid host by reading per-filter counts in the scheduler log.

q: What are flavors and how do you design them well?
a: A flavor defines the size of an instance: vCPUs, RAM, root disk, ephemeral disk and swap, plus extra specs that control behaviour. Extra specs can pin CPUs, request hugepages, set NUMA topology, request a trait through the trait prefix, or select an aggregate. Good flavor design keeps a small, predictable catalogue rather than hundreds of custom sizes, because each one fragments capacity. I group them into families, general purpose, compute optimised, memory optimised, and GPU, with consistent ratios of RAM to vCPU. Root disk sizes are small if instances boot from volume. I make dedicated-CPU flavors public only where needed, and I use private flavors for special tenants. Flavors are immutable in practice, so changing one means creating a new flavor and resizing instances, which is why planning them up front matters. Finally, I would say how I would document this for the team so the knowledge does not live only in one person's head.
f: How do you pin CPUs through a flavor?
Why prefer boot from volume with small root disks?
p: A flavor sets vCPU, RAM and disk, and extra specs add pinning, hugepages, traits and aggregate selection. Keep a small catalogue grouped by family to avoid capacity fragmentation.
tip: A short, consistent flavor catalogue is a capacity-planning argument, not just a UX one.

q: Explain the lifecycle and common states of a Nova instance.
a: An instance starts in BUILD while the scheduler, compute, image and network work completes. It becomes ACTIVE when running, SHUTOFF when stopped, and PAUSED or SUSPENDED when the guest is frozen in memory or saved to disk. ERROR means a task failed and the fault field tells you why. Transitional states like RESIZE, VERIFY_RESIZE, MIGRATING, REBUILD and SHELVED_OFFLOADED show an operation in flight, and the separate task state field shows exactly which step. SHELVED_OFFLOADED releases the hypervisor resources and keeps only an image, which is a good way to save capacity for idle servers. DELETED is final, with soft delete optional. In practice I always look at three fields together: status, task_state and power_state, because an instance can be ACTIVE in the database while the guest is actually shut off on the host, and that mismatch is a classic troubleshooting clue.
f: What does VERIFY_RESIZE mean?
How do you reset a stuck instance state?
p: BUILD, ACTIVE, SHUTOFF, PAUSED, SUSPENDED, SHELVED_OFFLOADED, ERROR and DELETED. Check status, task_state and power_state together; a mismatch points at a host-side problem.
cmds: openstack server show web1 -c status -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state -c OS-EXT-STS:power_state
tip: Mention power_state versus status mismatch: it signals the database and the hypervisor disagree.

q: How does cloud-init and the metadata service work in OpenStack?
a: When an instance boots, cloud-init inside the image asks for configuration at the well-known link-local address 169.254.169.254. Neutron makes this reachable through a metadata proxy, either in the router or DHCP namespace, or the OVN metadata agent, which forwards the request to the Nova metadata API and adds headers that identify the instance. Nova returns the hostname, SSH public key, user data and network details. Alternatively, a config drive can be attached as a small read-only disk containing the same data, which works even when there is no network or DHCP. User data is where you inject scripts or cloud-config YAML for first-boot setup. If an instance has no SSH key or user data did not run, I check whether it reached the metadata endpoint from inside the guest, then the metadata agent logs, then whether a config drive would be more reliable.
f: When would you prefer a config drive?
What breaks if the metadata agent is down?
p: cloud-init queries 169.254.169.254, which Neutron proxies to the Nova metadata API. A config drive is the no-network alternative. User data is the first-boot hook.
tip: Name both paths: the network metadata service and the config drive.

q: How are projects, quotas and limits managed, and what happens when a quota is hit?
a: Every resource belongs to a project, formerly called a tenant, and each project has quotas per service: instances, cores, RAM, volumes, gigabytes, floating IPs, security groups and so on. When a user asks for a resource, the service checks current usage against the quota and rejects the request with a quota exceeded error if it would be crossed. Operators set defaults and per-project overrides, and Nova and Cinder can use unified limits through Keystone for a consistent model. Quotas protect shared capacity and prevent one noisy tenant from consuming everything, but they are not guarantees of capacity. They do not reserve hardware. So I pair quotas with capacity monitoring, and I audit usage sync, because after failures the recorded usage can drift from reality and I may need to recount it for a project.
f: Does a quota reserve capacity?
How do you fix quota usage drift?
p: Quotas cap per-project consumption and are enforced at request time. They limit but do not reserve capacity, so combine them with real capacity monitoring.
tip: Be explicit that quota is a ceiling, not a reservation.

q: What is the service catalog and how do endpoints work?
a: The service catalog is the list Keystone returns inside a token response, telling clients where every service lives. Each service, such as compute or network, has endpoints for three interfaces: public, internal and admin, and for each region. Clients use the public endpoint, services talking to each other inside the cloud use the internal endpoint, and administrative operations may use the admin endpoint. This split lets you put public APIs behind a TLS-terminating load balancer with a public name while internal traffic stays on a private network. A common outage cause is a wrong endpoint URL, for example pointing to an old controller IP after a migration, which makes only some services fail. I verify with the catalog, confirm each URL responds, and make sure the region name matches between clients and services. I would finish by naming the one log line or metric that proves the change worked, because verification is what separates a confident answer from a guess.
f: Why separate internal and public endpoints?
What breaks when an endpoint URL is stale?
p: Keystone returns a catalog of services with public, internal and admin endpoints per region. Clients pick by interface and region, so a stale URL breaks only the services that use it.
tip: Mention interfaces and region together, since mismatches are the usual bug.

q: How do OpenStack microversions and API versioning work?
a: Most OpenStack APIs keep a stable major version, for example Compute v2.1, and add features through microversions. A client states the microversion it wants with a header such as X-OpenStack-Nova-API-Version, or the CLI flag os-compute-api-version. The server then behaves as defined for that microversion, and each new minor feature bumps the number. If the client asks for a version higher than the server supports, it gets a clear error, and if it omits the header it receives the baseline behaviour, which keeps old scripts working. The discovery document at the API root lists the minimum and maximum supported versions. For automation I pin an explicit microversion so behaviour does not change under me during upgrades, and I test upgrades by running the same scripts at the old and new maximum. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: Why pin a microversion in scripts?
How do you find the maximum supported version?
p: Stable major versions, with microversions adding behaviour. Clients opt in through a header; omitting it gives baseline behaviour. Pin the version in automation.
tip: Explain that pinning keeps automation stable across upgrades.

q: What is oslo and why do operators care about it?
a: Oslo is the set of shared Python libraries used by every OpenStack project, so each service does not reinvent the basics. The ones operators meet most are oslo.messaging for RPC over RabbitMQ, oslo.db for database access, oslo.config for configuration files, oslo.log for logging, oslo.policy for authorisation rules, and oslo.cache for caching. Because these are shared, behaviour is consistent: the same config option style, the same log format, the same retry semantics. It also means tuning oslo.messaging, for instance heartbeat and timeout settings, affects all services at once, and a bug there is cloud-wide. When I troubleshoot, I often start with oslo.messaging errors, because a message timeout in one service is usually a symptom of a broken queue, a dead consumer, or clock and network problems rather than a bug in that service itself. To make it concrete, I would describe a real situation where I applied this and what I measured before and after.
f: Which oslo option would you tune for RabbitMQ flaps?
How does oslo.policy relate to RBAC?
p: Oslo is the shared library layer: messaging, db, config, log, policy and cache. Tuning or bugs there affect every service, which is why messaging errors are the first thing to check.
tip: Say you read MessagingTimeout errors as a queue or consumer symptom, not a service bug.

q: How do you read and manage OpenStack configuration and logs effectively?
a: Each service reads an ini-style file such as nova.conf or neutron.conf, plus drop-in directories in newer releases, and some changes only apply after a restart while others support a mutable reload through SIGHUP. In containerised deployments like Kolla, the configuration is rendered by Ansible and mounted into containers, so I change it in the deployment tooling, never by hand on the host, otherwise the next run overwrites it. For logs, every service writes to its own file or to journald, and a request ID, req-uuid, is propagated across services so I can follow one API call from Nova to Neutron to Cinder. I ship logs to a central system, index by request ID and instance UUID, and keep debug off by default, switching it on for one service temporarily. Good logging discipline is half of OpenStack operations.
f: What is a request ID used for?
How do you enable debug temporarily?
p: ini files per service, reloaded by restart or SIGHUP. In containers, change configuration through the deployment tool. Follow one request across services with its req-id.
tip: The request ID across services is the single best debugging tool; mention it.

q: What does the release cycle look like and how do SLURP releases affect upgrades?
a: OpenStack ships a new release roughly every six months, named alphabetically, for example 2024.1 Caracal and 2024.2 Dalmatian. Each release is supported by the community for a limited maintenance window, with extended maintenance after that. Since 2023.1, the project introduced SLURP, Skip Level Upgrade Release Process, where every other release is designated a SLURP release, and you can upgrade directly from one SLURP release to the next, skipping the one between. That halves the number of upgrade events to roughly one per year while still allowing the intermediate non-SLURP releases for those who want newer features. For planning, I pick a SLURP path, test the upgrade in a staging cloud that mirrors production, read the release notes for removed options and deprecations, and schedule it as a rolling upgrade. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: What is the difference between SLURP and non-SLURP?
How do you test an upgrade safely?
p: Two releases a year; every other one is a SLURP release you can upgrade between directly, so one planned upgrade per year is possible.
tip: Mention you test the exact upgrade path in staging and read the removed-options notes.

q: How do you check the health of a running OpenStack cloud quickly?
a: I check in layers. First the control-plane services: openstack compute service list and network agent list show whether every nova-compute, scheduler, conductor and neutron agent is up. Second, the shared dependencies, which are Galera cluster size and sync state, RabbitMQ cluster status and queue depth, and the HAProxy backends. Third, a real functional probe: create a tiny instance, attach a floating IP, ping it and delete it, which exercises Keystone, Nova, Glance, Neutron and the data plane together. I automate that as a canary every few minutes. Fourth, resource headroom, meaning hypervisor usage, Ceph capacity and placement allocations. Fifth, logs and alerts for errors and stuck instances. A green service list with a failing canary tells you the problem is in the integration or data plane, not in a daemon. I always add that the right answer depends on the workload, so I would ask about scale and failure tolerance before committing to a design.
f: What would your canary test include?
Which metric tells you RabbitMQ is struggling?
p: Check service and agent lists, Galera and RabbitMQ state, run a synthetic canary that boots a VM and pings it, then check capacity headroom.
tip: A synthetic end-to-end canary catches what a green service list misses.

q: What is Horizon and when do you prefer the CLI, SDK or API instead?
a: Horizon is the Django web dashboard that lets users and admins manage projects, instances, networks and volumes, and it just calls the public APIs, so anything it does you can also do elsewhere. I use it for quick exploration and for users who are new to the cloud. For daily operations and automation I prefer the unified openstack CLI because it is scriptable and consistent across services, and for programmatic work I use openstacksdk in Python or the Terraform and Ansible providers, which give repeatable, reviewable infrastructure. Raw REST calls are mostly for debugging when I want to see headers and microversions. A key operational point is authentication: clouds.yaml keeps credentials and endpoints for multiple clouds and projects, so the same tooling works everywhere without sourcing environment files by hand. I would also mention the main failure mode and how I would detect it early, since operations experience shows in how you talk about what goes wrong.
f: What is clouds.yaml?
Why is infrastructure as code better than Horizon clicks?
p: Horizon is a UI over the same APIs. Use the openstack CLI for scripting, openstacksdk, Terraform or Ansible for repeatable automation, and clouds.yaml for credentials.
tip: Say that anything repeatable belongs in code, not in dashboard clicks.

q: How do images work in Glance and what formats do you use?
a: Glance stores and serves virtual machine images and their metadata. An image has a disk format, such as qcow2, raw, vmdk or iso, and a container format, usually bare. With a Ceph backend, I convert images to raw so that instances can be created as copy-on-write clones of the image in RBD, which makes boot take seconds instead of copying gigabytes. Images have visibility settings, private, shared, community or public, and properties like hw_disk_bus, hw_vif_model and os_distro that tell Nova how to present hardware to the guest. I keep golden images small, patched regularly, with cloud-init installed and no secrets inside, and I sign them where possible. Glance also supports multiple backends and image caching on compute hosts for speed. I would finish by naming the one log line or metric that proves the change worked, because verification is what separates a confident answer from a guess.
f: Why raw images on Ceph?
How do you control who can see an image?
p: Glance stores images with format and metadata properties. On Ceph, use raw so boots are instant copy-on-write clones. Keep golden images small, patched and secret-free.
cmds: openstack image create --disk-format raw --container-format bare --file ubuntu.raw --public ubuntu-22.04
qemu-img convert -f qcow2 -O raw ubuntu.qcow2 ubuntu.raw
tip: The raw-on-Ceph point shows you understand the storage and compute interaction.

q: Explain live migration: how it works, its requirements and common failures.
a: Live migration moves a running instance between compute hosts with minimal downtime. Libvirt copies the guest memory pages iteratively to the destination while the guest keeps running, then briefly pauses it, transfers the last dirty pages and the CPU state, and resumes it on the target. With shared storage such as Ceph, only memory moves. Without shared storage, block migration also copies the disk, which is much slower. Requirements are compatible CPU models between hosts, reachable libvirt and migration ports, consistent networking, matching image and volume access, and enough destination capacity. Common failures include CPU feature mismatches, a guest dirtying memory faster than it can be copied so it never converges, firewalls blocking ports, and mismatched Neutron port binding. Tools to help include auto-converge, post-copy and a configurable downtime limit. The key point I want the interviewer to hear is that I understand the trade-off, not just the definition.
f: How do you handle a guest that never converges?
What CPU mode do you set for migration-friendly clouds?
p: Libvirt pre-copies memory while the guest runs, then pauses briefly to finish and resume on the target. Shared storage keeps it quick; CPU model mismatches and high dirty rates are common failures.
tip: Name auto-converge and post-copy as the answer for busy guests.

q: What is the difference between cold migration, resize, evacuate and rebuild?
a: They look similar but serve different situations. Cold migration shuts the instance down, moves it to another host and starts it again, and is used for maintenance when live migration is not possible. Resize changes the flavor, and because the new size may not fit the old host, it also moves the instance; the state VERIFY_RESIZE lets the user confirm or revert. Evacuate is for failure: when a compute host is dead, you rebuild its instances on another host, keeping the same UUID, network ports and volumes, and for shared-storage setups the disk survives. Rebuild reinstalls an instance from a new or same image on the same host, wiping the root disk. Picking the right one is a classic scenario question, with the key words being planned versus failed host, and keep data versus reinstall.
f: What data is lost on rebuild?
What must be true before you evacuate?
p: Cold migrate: planned move with downtime. Resize: new flavor, may move. Evacuate: recover from a dead host. Rebuild: reinstall the root disk from an image.
tip: Frame it as planned versus failed host, and data kept versus wiped.

q: What is CPU pinning and NUMA awareness, and when do you need them?
a: Modern servers have multiple NUMA nodes, where memory and PCI devices are closer to certain cores. A guest that spans nodes pays a latency penalty for remote memory. With the flavor property hw:cpu_policy set to dedicated, Nova pins each guest vCPU to a specific host physical core, and with hw:numa_nodes it keeps the guest on specified NUMA nodes, aligning memory and vCPUs. Combined with hugepages, this gives predictable low latency and is standard for telco, NFV, databases and high-performance workloads. The trade-off is that pinned instances cannot be overcommitted and reduce scheduling flexibility, so I place them in a dedicated host aggregate, reserve host cores for the OS using cpu_dedicated_set and cpu_shared_set, and use separate flavors. For ordinary web workloads, shared CPUs with overcommit are the better cost choice. If the interviewer pushes further, I would explain how I would test this in a staging environment before touching production.
f: Why separate dedicated and shared CPU sets?
What does hw:cpu_thread_policy do?
p: hw:cpu_policy=dedicated pins vCPUs to cores and NUMA settings keep memory local. Great for latency-sensitive loads, but no overcommit, so isolate with aggregates.
cmds: openstack flavor set rt --property hw:cpu_policy=dedicated --property hw:numa_nodes=1
tip: State the trade-off: performance and predictability versus density.

q: How do hugepages help, and how are they configured for instances?
a: Normal memory uses 4 KB pages, so large guests need many page-table entries, and the CPU translation cache, the TLB, misses often. Hugepages, typically 2 MB or 1 GB, cut that overhead and improve memory-intensive and packet-processing workloads, and they are required for DPDK. On the host you reserve hugepages at boot with kernel parameters, so they are not fragmented, and you tell Nova how much memory is for hugepages. On the instance side you set the flavor property hw:mem_page_size to large, 2MB or 1GB. Hugepage memory is not swappable and not shared with normal allocations, so you must size reservations carefully; too many starves normal guests and the host, too few causes scheduling failures. I also remember that guests with hugepages cannot use memory overcommit. I always add that the right answer depends on the workload, so I would ask about scale and failure tolerance before committing to a design.
f: Why are hugepages needed for DPDK?
What happens if hugepages are exhausted?
p: Hugepages reduce TLB misses for big or packet-heavy guests. Reserve them at host boot, set hw:mem_page_size on the flavor, and accept no memory overcommit.
tip: Link hugepages to DPDK and NFV to show you know the use case.

q: How do CPU and RAM overcommit ratios work and how do you choose them?
a: Overcommit lets the scheduler allocate more virtual resources than physical ones, because most guests are idle most of the time. The cpu_allocation_ratio and ram_allocation_ratio are set per compute node, or through Placement inventory, with typical defaults of 16 for CPU and 1.5 for RAM. CPU overcommit is relatively safe because the kernel scheduler time-slices, but it hurts latency under contention; I watch steal time and load. RAM overcommit is riskier, because exhausting host memory triggers swapping or the OOM killer, so I use a low ratio like 1.0 to 1.2 for production. Disk can be overcommitted with thin provisioning but needs monitoring. I choose ratios by workload class, conservative for databases and latency-sensitive tenants, higher for dev and test aggregates, and I confirm with real utilisation data, not guesses. To make it concrete, I would describe a real situation where I applied this and what I measured before and after.
f: Which metric shows CPU contention?
Where do you set the ratio so it is respected by Placement?
p: Allocation ratios let scheduling exceed physical capacity. CPU 4 to 16 is common, RAM close to 1. Set per aggregate by workload and watch steal time and memory pressure.
cmds: openstack resource provider inventory show <uuid> VCPU
tip: Say conservative for databases, aggressive for dev, and validate with steal time.

q: What are Nova cells v2 and why would you deploy them?
a: Cells v2 is Nova's horizontal scaling design. The top level has the API database, which holds instance mappings and host mappings, and the API services. Below that, each cell has its own database and message queue, serving a group of compute nodes. A request is routed to a cell by the scheduler and conductor, and the instance data lives in that cell. This bounds the size of any one RabbitMQ cluster and database, which are the usual bottlenecks at a few thousand compute nodes, and it gives a failure domain, since a broken cell affects only its hosts. There is always at least cell0, which holds instances that failed to schedule, and a default cell1. I would introduce extra cells when node counts, message rates or upgrade blast radius justify the added complexity. Finally, I would say how I would document this for the team so the knowledge does not live only in one person's head.
f: What is cell0 for?
Which services run per cell versus globally?
p: Cells split compute nodes into groups with their own DB and queue under a global API database. They bound RabbitMQ and DB load and limit failure blast radius.
tip: Cells are about bounding the message bus and DB, not about regions.

q: A compute node dies. What is your recovery procedure?
a: First confirm it is really down, not just a service issue, by checking the host, the hypervisor in nova and the console or BMC. If it is dead, I fence it so it cannot come back and corrupt shared disks, which is critical with shared storage. I mark the service forced down so Nova stops waiting for it, then evacuate the instances to healthy hosts, either one by one or in bulk with the host-evacuate approach. Instances on shared storage such as Ceph keep their disk and boot again with the same identity. Instances on local ephemeral disk lose data, so I tell the owners. I then check that ports, volumes and floating IPs are re-bound, repair or replace the hardware, and re-enable the service. Afterwards I review why detection and recovery were not automatic and add monitoring or Masakari.
f: Why fence before evacuate?
What is Masakari?
p: Verify the failure, fence the host, force the service down, evacuate instances (shared storage preserves disks), verify networking, then repair and re-enable. Automate with Masakari.
tip: Always say fencing comes before evacuation; that is the data-safety point.

q: How do server groups and affinity rules work?
a: A server group is a policy container that you attach to instances at boot using a scheduler hint. The policies are affinity, which places all members on the same host, anti-affinity, which forces them onto different hosts, and the soft variants that try but do not fail the build. The common use is high availability: put the replicas of a database or a stateless tier into an anti-affinity group so one host failure cannot take them all out. The limitation is that anti-affinity needs enough hosts, so a strict group of five on a three-host cloud will fail with no valid host. Also, the rule is enforced at build and during live migration and evacuate, which can block maintenance. I use soft anti-affinity when capacity is tight, and strict where the application truly cannot survive co-location.
f: What is the difference between anti-affinity and soft anti-affinity?
How does anti-affinity affect maintenance?
p: Server groups with anti-affinity spread replicas across hosts and affinity co-locates them. Strict policies fail when hosts run out, so use the soft variant when capacity is tight.
cmds: openstack server group create --policy anti-affinity db-group
openstack server create --hint group=<group-id> --flavor m1.large --image ubuntu db1
tip: Mention that strict anti-affinity can block live migration during maintenance.

q: How do you provide GPUs to instances: passthrough versus vGPU?
a: There are two main approaches. With PCI passthrough, a whole physical GPU is assigned to one instance through VFIO, giving near native performance but no sharing. You enable IOMMU, whitelist the device in nova.conf, create a flavor with a pci alias, and Nova schedules onto hosts with a free device. With vGPU, an NVIDIA or similar driver splits one card into mdev types, and Nova assigns those virtual devices to several instances, which raises utilisation and suits VDI and smaller inference jobs, though it needs vendor licences and has migration limits. I choose passthrough for heavy training and full-card workloads, and vGPU for shared, smaller workloads. Either way I put GPU hosts in a dedicated aggregate, tag them with traits so the scheduler is precise, and monitor temperature, memory and utilisation with the vendor exporter.
f: What is needed on the host for passthrough?
What are the migration limits of vGPU?
p: Passthrough gives a whole GPU to one guest with full performance. vGPU shares a card across guests. Use aggregates and traits to schedule precisely.
tip: State the trade-off: dedicated performance versus utilisation.

q: An instance is stuck in a transitional state such as BUILD or deleting. How do you fix it?
a: First I find out why, not just reset it. I look at the instance fault and task_state, then the nova-compute log on the host, using the request ID, to see what step hung: maybe image download, a Neutron port that never became active, a Cinder attach, or a libvirt error. If the underlying operation is gone, for example the compute service restarted mid-task, the database still shows the old task state, and the safe cleanup is to reset the state with openstack server set --state error, then delete or rebuild it. For a stuck delete I check for leftover ports, volumes and libvirt domains, which often block cleanup. I avoid editing the database directly except as a documented last resort. Afterwards I add a periodic job or alert for instances in the same state over a time threshold.
f: What is the safe way to reset an instance?
How do you detect stuck instances proactively?
p: Read fault, task_state and the compute log by request ID to learn what hung. Then reset state to error and delete or rebuild; clean up ports and volumes. Alert on long-lived transitional states.
cmds: openstack server show web1 -c fault -c OS-EXT-STS:task_state
tip: Diagnose before resetting; resetting hides the cause.

q: What hypervisors does Nova support and why is KVM the default choice?
a: Nova supports several drivers through a compute driver interface. KVM through libvirt is by far the most used, and it is the best-tested path with all features such as live migration, NUMA, hugepages, vGPU and SR-IOV. Others include QEMU in pure emulation for testing, VMware vCenter, where Nova talks to vSphere, Hyper-V, and Ironic for bare metal instead of virtual machines. LXC and Virtuozzo drivers exist but see far less use. I choose KVM because it is open source, integrated in the Linux kernel, supported by every major distribution, performs close to bare metal with hardware virtualisation, and has the strongest community and vendor support. The decision to use VMware as a Nova backend usually comes from an existing investment, but then you lose several OpenStack-native features. Finally, I would say how I would document this for the team so the knowledge does not live only in one person's head.
f: When would you use the VMware driver?
What does Ironic add?
p: KVM via libvirt is the mainstream, best-tested driver. Others exist, such as VMware, Hyper-V and Ironic for bare metal, but KVM has the richest feature support.
tip: Answer with KVM and give one reason beyond cost, such as feature coverage.

q: How do you perform maintenance on a compute node without user impact?
a: I plan it as a controlled drain. First I disable the compute service so the scheduler stops placing new instances there, with a reason recorded. Then I live-migrate instances away, in batches, checking that each migration completes and the guest remains reachable. Instances that cannot be live-migrated, such as those with pinned devices, get coordinated downtime or a cold migration with the owner informed. Once empty, I perform the work, such as a kernel patch, firmware update or hardware fix, then reboot, verify libvirt, nova-compute and the Neutron agent are healthy, and re-enable the service. For large fleets I use host aggregates and automation with Ansible, and I respect anti-affinity groups and capacity so the drain does not overload remaining hosts. Communication and a rollback plan complete the procedure. I would finish by naming the one log line or metric that proves the change worked, because verification is what separates a confident answer from a guess.
f: What can block a drain?
How do you automate the loop for many hosts?
p: Disable the service, live-migrate instances in batches, handle non-migratable guests with coordination, do the work, verify agents, re-enable. Watch capacity and anti-affinity.
cmds: openstack compute service set --disable --disable-reason 'kernel patch' <host> nova-compute
openstack server list --host <host> --all-projects -f value -c ID | xargs -n1 openstack server migrate --live-migration
tip: Say disable first, drain, work, verify, enable, in that order.

q: Explain the Neutron architecture: server, ML2 plugin, agents and mechanism drivers.
a: Neutron is the networking service. The neutron-server exposes the API and stores networks, subnets, ports and routers in the database. It uses the ML2 plugin, a modular framework with type drivers, which define how a network is built, such as flat, vlan, vxlan or geneve, and mechanism drivers, which actually program the back end, such as Open vSwitch, Linux bridge or OVN. In the classic OVS design, agents run on every node: the OVS agent wires ports, the DHCP agent runs dnsmasq per network, the L3 agent runs routers in namespaces, and the metadata agent proxies instance metadata. In the OVN design most of that logic moves into the OVN databases and ovn-controller on each host. I explain it as control plane in neutron-server and a data plane implemented by whichever mechanism driver you choose.
f: What does a type driver do versus a mechanism driver?
Which agents disappear with OVN?
p: neutron-server holds the API and DB; ML2 combines type drivers (flat, vlan, vxlan, geneve) with mechanism drivers (OVS, OVN, Linux bridge) that program the data plane; agents run per node.
tip: Separate control plane (server and DB) from data plane (driver) in the answer.

q: OVS versus OVN: what changed and why do most new clouds choose OVN?
a: ML2 with Open vSwitch uses a set of Python agents on every node: the OVS agent, L3 agent, DHCP agent and metadata agent, communicating over RabbitMQ, and routers run as Linux namespaces, which adds control-plane chatter and scale limits. OVN, Open Virtual Network, moves logical networking into a dedicated database model. Neutron writes logical switches, routers, ACLs and ports to the OVN northbound database, ovn-northd translates them into logical flows in the southbound database, and ovn-controller on each hypervisor programs OVS locally. Routing and security groups become OpenFlow rules distributed on every host, so DVR style east-west routing is built in, DHCP and metadata are handled by ovn-controller, and RabbitMQ load drops. The benefits are better scale, simpler operations and fewer moving parts, which is why new clouds default to OVN. To make it concrete, I would describe a real situation where I applied this and what I measured before and after.
f: What are the northbound and southbound databases?
How do you migrate from OVS to OVN?
p: OVN replaces the agent-based design with logical networking in OVN databases, ovn-northd translation and ovn-controller on each host. Fewer agents, less RabbitMQ chatter, distributed routing by default.
tip: Name northd and ovn-controller to show you know the pipeline.

q: What is the difference between provider networks and tenant (self-service) networks?
a: Provider networks map directly onto physical networks that the operator defined, typically flat or VLAN, and instances attach to them like machines on the data-centre network. They are created by admins, have real routable addresses, and use the external router, so performance is simple and predictable, and they are common for production and for telco. Tenant networks, also called self-service, are created by users inside their project, usually as VXLAN or Geneve overlays, and are connected to external networks by a virtual router with SNAT and floating IPs. They give isolation and self-service, overlapping address ranges between tenants, and no involvement from the network team, at the cost of encapsulation overhead and a more complex data path. Many clouds use both: tenant networks for general workloads and provider networks for workloads that need direct addressing.
f: Why can tenants overlap IP ranges?
When would you offer provider networks to tenants?
p: Provider networks are operator-defined mappings to physical VLANs with routable addresses. Tenant networks are user-created overlays routed to the outside through a virtual router and floating IPs.
cmds: openstack network create --provider-network-type vlan --provider-physical-network physnet1 --provider-segment 120 prov120
tip: Give a use case for each: provider for direct addressing, tenant for self-service isolation.

q: How do VXLAN and Geneve overlays work, and what is the MTU consequence?
a: An overlay wraps each guest Ethernet frame inside a UDP packet that travels over the underlay between hypervisors. VXLAN uses a 24-bit virtual network identifier, so you can have about sixteen million segments instead of 4094 VLANs, with UDP port 4789. Geneve is the more extensible successor used by OVN, with variable-length options that carry metadata such as logical port identifiers. The cost is overhead: VXLAN adds about 50 bytes, Geneve about 58 or more, so if the underlay MTU is 1500 the guest MTU must be lowered to about 1442, otherwise large packets are fragmented or dropped, and you see the classic symptom of small requests working while large transfers hang. The fix is either a larger underlay MTU, such as 9000 jumbo frames, or advertising the correct smaller MTU to instances through DHCP.
f: How would you detect an MTU mismatch?
Why jumbo frames on the underlay?
p: Overlays encapsulate guest frames in UDP between hypervisors, adding 50 to 58 bytes of header. Raise the underlay MTU or lower the guest MTU, or large packets will hang.
tip: The symptom-based answer: small packets work, big ones hang.

q: What is DVR and when is it useful with OVS ML2?
a: Distributed Virtual Routing moves the L3 function from a few central network nodes onto every compute node. Without it, all routed traffic and all floating IP traffic hairpin through the network node, creating a bottleneck and single point of failure. With DVR, east-west traffic between subnets is routed locally on the compute node, and north-south traffic for instances with floating IPs goes directly out from the compute node through a floating IP namespace, while instances without floating IPs still use centralised SNAT on a network node. It improves scale and latency, but it adds complexity, more namespaces, more agents and harder debugging, and it requires external connectivity on compute nodes. With OVN this distributed behaviour is built in, so DVR is mainly a topic for ML2 OVS clouds. I always add that the right answer depends on the workload, so I would ask about scale and failure tolerance before committing to a design.
f: Which traffic still goes through the network node?
How does OVN change this?
p: DVR runs routers on compute nodes so east-west and floating IP traffic avoid the network node bottleneck. Centralised SNAT remains for instances without floating IPs. OVN does this natively.
cmds: ip netns exec qrouter-<id> ip a
tip: Say what remains centralised, which shows depth.

q: How do floating IPs and SNAT work for instances?
a: A private instance sends traffic to its subnet gateway, which is a Neutron router. For outbound traffic without a floating IP, the router performs source NAT, replacing the instance address with the router's external gateway address, so many instances share one public IP. A floating IP is a one-to-one NAT mapping: Neutron associates a public address from an external network pool with the instance port, and the router performs DNAT for inbound traffic and SNAT for outbound traffic using that address. The instance itself never sees the public address, only its private one. Security groups still apply to the private port, so you must allow inbound traffic there. For troubleshooting I check the router namespace NAT rules, the external gateway, the instance security group, and whether the upstream network knows how to reach the floating range, often through ARP or BGP.
f: Why do floating IPs fail even when the association exists?
How is the floating pool routed upstream?
p: Routers SNAT outbound traffic and floating IPs add one-to-one DNAT and SNAT. Instances keep private addresses and security groups apply to the private port.
cmds: openstack server add floating ip web1 203.0.113.10
ip netns exec qrouter-<id> iptables -t nat -S | grep 203.0.113.10
tip: Remember to say the upstream network must route the floating range.

q: How do security groups work and how are they implemented?
a: A security group is a set of stateful allow rules attached to a port. By default all inbound traffic is denied and all outbound is allowed, and you add rules by direction, protocol, port range, and either a CIDR or another security group as the source, which is very useful for tier-to-tier rules such as allowing the app group to reach the database group. Because they are stateful, return traffic is permitted automatically through connection tracking. In ML2 OVS, rules become iptables or OVS flows with conntrack on the compute host, in the native OVS firewall driver, and in OVN they are ACLs translated into logical flows. Port security also adds anti-spoofing, preventing a guest from sending packets with another MAC or IP address. For debugging, I check the rules, the attached groups on the port, and the conntrack entries on the host.
f: Why reference a security group as a source?
How do you disable port security for an NFV instance?
p: Stateful allow-only rules attached to ports, with default deny inbound. Implemented as conntrack-based OVS flows or OVN ACLs; port security blocks spoofing.
cmds: openstack security group rule create --protocol tcp --dst-port 443 --remote-group app-sg db-sg
tip: Mention group-to-group rules, which scale better than CIDR lists.

q: What is Octavia and how does it provide load balancing as a service?
a: Octavia is the load-balancing service for OpenStack. When a user creates a load balancer, a listener, a pool and members, the Octavia controller builds an amphora, which is a small virtual machine running HAProxy and keepalived, in a management network, and configures it through a REST agent. In active-standby topology two amphorae share a virtual IP using VRRP, so a failure of one is handled automatically. Octavia supports L4 and L7 policies, TLS termination with certificates stored in Barbican, health monitors, and since newer releases, a provider framework with OVN as a lightweight L4 provider that avoids amphora VMs. For Kubernetes on OpenStack, the cloud provider uses Octavia to create service type LoadBalancer. Operationally I watch amphora health, image updates, the management network, and quota for the load balancer project. The key point I want the interviewer to hear is that I understand the trade-off, not just the definition.
f: What is an amphora?
When would you use the OVN provider instead?
p: Octavia creates HAProxy-based amphora VMs, optionally in active-standby with VRRP, and offers L4/L7, TLS termination and health monitors. The OVN provider is a lightweight L4 option.
cmds: openstack loadbalancer listener create --protocol HTTPS --protocol-port 443 lb1
tip: Link Octavia to Kubernetes services of type LoadBalancer.

q: An instance does not get an IP address from DHCP. How do you troubleshoot?
a: I work from the guest outward. First I check the instance console log to see whether the DHCP client ran and what it sent. Second, I confirm the port is ACTIVE and bound to the expected host, because a port in DOWN or binding failed means the data plane is not wired. Third, I verify the DHCP agent or OVN DHCP is alive for that network, that the subnet has DHCP enabled and free addresses, and that the port's MAC and IP are registered. Fourth, I capture traffic on the tap interface, the integration bridge and the dnsmasq namespace, looking for the DISCOVER and OFFER. Common causes are security group rules or port security blocking, an overlay MTU problem, a down agent, an exhausted subnet, or a mismatched VLAN on a provider network. I fix the specific layer and retest.
f: How do you capture on a tap device?
What if only some instances fail?
p: Check console log, port status and binding, DHCP agent and subnet state, then capture DISCOVER/OFFER on tap, bridge and namespace. Usual culprits: agent down, binding failure, MTU, VLAN, exhausted pool.
cmds: ip netns exec qdhcp-<net> tcpdump -ni any port 67 or port 68
tip: Narrate layer by layer: guest, port, agent, wire.

q: What does a Neutron port binding failure mean and how do you fix it?
a: When an instance boots, Nova asks Neutron to bind the port to the chosen host. Neutron's ML2 asks each mechanism driver whether it can bind that port on that host for a network of that type. If none can, the port ends in binding_failed, and the instance goes to ERROR. Typical causes are an agent that is down or not reporting on that host, a missing or misnamed physical network mapping such as bridge_mappings, a network type that the host does not support, or a mechanism driver misconfiguration, for example an SR-IOV request on a host without VFs. I read the port's binding profile and vif_type, check agent status on the host, compare the physnet name with the host configuration, and look at the neutron-server log for the reason. After fixing the cause, I rebuild or recreate the instance.
f: Where is physical network mapping configured?
How can the host agent list help?
p: Binding fails when no mechanism driver can bind the port on that host: agent down, wrong physnet mapping or unsupported network type. Inspect vif_type, agent state and server logs.
tip: Say vif_type=binding_failed and then check agent, physnet, type.

q: How do you debug network paths using namespaces, tcpdump and flows?
a: I follow the packet through each hop. On the compute host the path is guest, tap or vhost-user device, integration bridge br-int, then the tunnel bridge or provider bridge, and out to the physical NIC. I start with ip link and bridge checks, then use tcpdump on the tap and on the physical interface to see where packets stop. For routers and DHCP in ML2 OVS, I enter the network namespace with ip netns exec and run ip, iptables and tcpdump inside it. For flow-level problems, I use ovs-ofctl dump-flows and ovs-appctl ofproto/trace to simulate a packet and show which rule matches. With OVN, ovn-trace does the same for logical flows. Comparing where a packet is seen last tells me which component is dropping it. The key point I want the interviewer to hear is that I understand the trade-off, not just the definition.
f: What does ofproto/trace give you?
How do you capture on a vhost-user interface?
p: Trace hop by hop: tap, br-int, tunnel or provider bridge, NIC. Use ip netns exec for routers and DHCP, and ovs-appctl ofproto/trace or ovn-trace to find the dropping rule.
cmds: ip netns exec qrouter-<id> tcpdump -ni any icmp
tip: The last hop where you still see the packet is where it gets dropped.

q: What is SR-IOV and how do you use it with OpenStack?
a: SR-IOV lets a physical NIC present multiple virtual functions, each a lightweight PCIe device that can be assigned directly to a guest, bypassing the host's virtual switch. This gives near line rate throughput and low latency with little CPU use, which suits NFV, telco and high-throughput workloads. In OpenStack you enable VFs on the NIC and IOMMU in the BIOS and kernel, whitelist the physical network in the Nova PCI configuration, enable the sriovnicswitch mechanism driver in Neutron with the SR-IOV agent, and create ports with vnic_type direct. The trade-offs are significant: no software security groups on the data path in many setups, limited live migration support, hardware-specific drivers in the guest, and fewer overlay features. I use it where performance justifies those constraints, and keep a normal OVS path for everything else. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: Why is live migration hard with SR-IOV?
What replaces security groups here?
p: SR-IOV assigns NIC virtual functions straight to guests for near line-rate networking. Use vnic_type direct, whitelist in Nova, and accept limits on migration and software filtering.
cmds: openstack port create --vnic-type direct --network sriov-net sriov-port
tip: State the trade-off: speed versus features such as migration and filtering.

q: How does Neutron QoS work and what can it limit?
a: The QoS extension lets you define policies with rules and attach them to ports or networks. Supported rule types include bandwidth limit, which caps egress or ingress rate, minimum bandwidth, which guarantees capacity and is enforced through Placement so the scheduler considers it, DSCP marking to set packet priority, and packet rate limits. The back end enforces it: OVS uses ingress policing and queues, OVN uses meters and QoS tables, and SR-IOV applies limits on the virtual function. I use QoS to stop one tenant saturating an uplink, to provide tiered network service levels, and to protect latency-sensitive traffic with DSCP. The limitations are that enforcement depends on the driver, that ingress and egress behave differently, and that without a minimum bandwidth guarantee QoS only restricts but does not promise capacity. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: How does minimum bandwidth interact with Placement?
Which direction is easier to limit?
p: QoS policies attach bandwidth, minimum bandwidth, DSCP and packet-rate rules to ports or networks. Enforcement depends on the driver, and minimum guarantees need Placement support.
cmds: openstack network qos policy create gold
openstack network qos rule create --type bandwidth-limit --max-kbps 100000 --egress gold
tip: Distinguish limits from guarantees.

q: What are trunk ports and when are they needed?
a: A trunk port carries traffic for several VLANs over a single virtual NIC. The parent port belongs to one network, and subports are attached with VLAN IDs, so the guest sees tagged frames and can create VLAN subinterfaces for each. This is needed for workloads that expect to be multi-homed through VLANs, such as NFV appliances, virtual routers and firewalls, and for Kubernetes or container platforms running inside a VM where pods get their own Neutron networks, as with Kuryr. It saves you from hot-plugging many separate ports, which hit hypervisor PCI slot limits. Operationally, you create the parent port, add subports with segmentation type vlan and ID, and in the guest configure matching VLAN interfaces. I verify tags at the bridge level if packets are missing. If the interviewer pushes further, I would explain how I would test this in a staging environment before touching production.
f: How does the guest need to be configured?
Why not just add many NICs?
p: A trunk carries multiple tagged VLANs on one vNIC via a parent port and subports. Used by NFV appliances and nested container networking to avoid many NICs.
cmds: openstack network trunk create --parent-port p0 trunk0
ip link add link eth0 name eth0.101 type vlan id 101
tip: Mention Kuryr or NFV as the real-world use.

q: How do you handle IPv6 and dual stack in OpenStack?
a: Neutron supports IPv6 subnets with either SLAAC, DHCPv6 stateless or stateful modes, controlled by ipv6_ra_mode and ipv6_address_mode. Router advertisements are generated by the router or the OVN logical router so guests configure addresses automatically. For dual stack, a network has both an IPv4 and an IPv6 subnet and ports receive both. There is no NAT for IPv6 by default, so instances get globally routable addresses, which means security groups become the primary protection, and the upstream network must route the prefix, either through static routes or BGP dynamic routing and prefix delegation. Common problems are forgetting IPv6 rules in security groups, an upstream that does not route the tenant prefix, and images that do not run an IPv6 client. I test with ping6 and a real application, not only router advertisements. I would round off by noting what I would automate here, because repeatable steps should not depend on memory.
f: Why do security groups matter more for IPv6?
What does prefix delegation provide?
p: IPv6 uses SLAAC or DHCPv6 with router advertisements. Dual stack gives both address families; there is no NAT, so security groups and upstream routing of the prefix are essential.
cmds: openstack subnet create --ip-version 6 --ipv6-ra-mode slaac --ipv6-address-mode slaac --network n1 --subnet-range 2001:db8:1::/64 v6
openstack security group rule create --ethertype IPv6 --protocol icmpv6 default
tip: Point out that no NAT shifts protection to security groups.

q: How does Neutron integrate with BGP and dynamic routing?
a: For public address space, the upstream needs to know where tenant or floating prefixes live. Neutron dynamic routing provides a BGP speaker that advertises tenant subnets and floating IPs to physical routers, so you do not maintain static routes. It uses address scopes and subnet pools to make sure only the right prefixes are advertised. With OVN, a BGP agent for OVN or an integration with FRR can advertise routes directly from each compute host, enabling routed networks where each rack is its own L3 domain, which avoids large stretched L2 segments and gives better scalability and failure isolation. I use this in leaf-spine fabrics: addresses are announced from where they live, ECMP gives load balancing, and failure convergence is handled by the routing protocol instead of VRRP or ARP tricks. I always add that the right answer depends on the workload, so I would ask about scale and failure tolerance before committing to a design.
f: What are address scopes for?
Why prefer routed networks over stretched L2?
p: Neutron BGP speakers or OVN with FRR advertise tenant and floating prefixes to the fabric, enabling routed leaf-spine designs without stretched L2 or static routes.
tip: Say leaf-spine with ECMP and per-rack L3 domains.

q: What are Designate and DNS integration in Neutron?
a: Designate is the DNS as a service project. Users create zones and recordsets through an API, and Designate publishes them to authoritative servers such as BIND or PowerDNS through a pool configuration. Neutron integrates with it so that when a port or floating IP is created, a DNS record is created automatically, for example web1.example.org pointing to the instance address, using the dns_name and dns_domain attributes, and removed again on deletion. This avoids manual DNS and stale records, and provides internal names for instances in a project. For internal resolution inside a tenant, Neutron DHCP can also serve DNS through dnsmasq with a configured forwarder. In production I decide who owns each zone, keep tenant zones separate from platform zones, and monitor propagation and the sink service that listens to notifications. To make it concrete, I would describe a real situation where I applied this and what I measured before and after.
f: What is the Designate sink?
How do you keep tenants from creating records in platform zones?
p: Designate offers DNS as a service publishing to BIND or PowerDNS. Neutron integration creates and removes records for ports and floating IPs automatically.
tip: Mention zone ownership and delegation for tenants.

q: How do you design the physical network for an OpenStack cloud?
a: I separate traffic types, usually into management, API, tunnel or overlay, storage, and external or provider networks, either as separate VLANs on bonded NICs or on separate physical interfaces. Storage traffic, especially Ceph, gets its own high-bandwidth and ideally non-oversubscribed path, with a separate replication network. The overlay network needs a larger MTU. Each node has redundant NICs in LACP or active-backup bonds connected to two top-of-rack switches in MLAG or a leaf-spine fabric with ECMP. The control plane sits on a stable L2 or L3 segment with a virtual IP managed by keepalived. I plan IP address ranges, VLAN ranges, firewalling between planes, and capacity with oversubscription ratios. Documenting the design as a diagram and an addressing table is as important as the hardware, because troubleshooting depends on it. The key point I want the interviewer to hear is that I understand the trade-off, not just the definition.
f: Why separate storage and tenant traffic?
What bonding mode would you use?
p: Separate management, API, overlay, storage and provider traffic; bond NICs across two ToR switches; jumbo MTU for overlay and storage; plan IPs and VLANs and document them.
tip: Lead with traffic separation, then redundancy, then MTU.

q: What is the metadata proxy path and why do some instances fail to get SSH keys?
a: Instances request metadata from 169.254.169.254. In ML2 OVS the request reaches a metadata proxy running in the router or DHCP namespace, which adds the instance and network identity and forwards it over a Unix socket to the neutron-metadata-agent, then to the Nova metadata API with a shared secret signature. In OVN the ovn-metadata-agent on each host serves this through a namespace and haproxy. Failures leave cloud-init with no key or user data. Causes include a missing route or DHCP option for the link-local address, the metadata agent being down, a shared secret mismatch between Neutron and Nova, a security group blocking egress to the address, or the Nova metadata API being unreachable. I curl the endpoint from inside the guest through a console, then walk the chain, agent, secret, Nova API. To make it concrete, I would describe a real situation where I applied this and what I measured before and after.
f: What is the shared secret for?
How does a config drive avoid all this?
p: 169.254.169.254 requests go through a namespace proxy and the metadata agent to Nova metadata, signed with a shared secret. Failures: agent down, secret mismatch, routing or egress blocked.
tip: Name the shared-secret mismatch, a classic cause.

q: Explain the Cinder architecture and how a volume is created and attached.
a: Cinder provides persistent block storage. The cinder-api accepts requests, the scheduler chooses a back end, based on capacity, volume type and extra specs, and cinder-volume runs per back end, talking to the actual storage system, such as Ceph RBD, LVM, NetApp or Pure, through a driver. When a user creates a volume, the scheduler picks a back end, and the driver allocates it. When the volume is attached to an instance, Nova asks Cinder to export it and returns connection information, then os-brick on the compute node connects it, using iSCSI, NVMe over TCP, Fibre Channel or RBD, and libvirt presents it as a virtual disk. Detach reverses this. Because the volume is independent of the instance, data survives deletion of the server. Key operational points are multiple back ends, volume types to map service classes, and keeping the driver and os-brick versions compatible with the storage array.
f: What does os-brick do?
What is a volume type?
p: API, scheduler and per-backend cinder-volume with a driver. Attach goes through Nova and os-brick on the compute host. Volumes outlive instances.
cmds: openstack server add volume web1 data1
tip: Mention os-brick as the glue on the compute side.

q: Why is Ceph the most common storage back end for OpenStack?
a: Ceph provides one unified, distributed storage cluster for several OpenStack needs: RBD block devices for Cinder volumes, Nova ephemeral disks and Glance images, RGW for S3 and Swift compatible object storage, and CephFS for shared file systems with Manila. It has no single point of failure, scales horizontally by adding OSD nodes, and data is spread across the cluster with the CRUSH algorithm and protected by replication, typically three copies, or erasure coding for cost efficiency. Because Nova, Glance and Cinder share the same RBD pools, creating a volume or instance from an image is a copy-on-write clone that is almost instant, and live migration works without copying disks. The costs are operational complexity, network requirements, and the need for good capacity planning and monitoring of placement groups, recovery traffic and OSD health. I would finish by naming the one log line or metric that proves the change worked, because verification is what separates a confident answer from a guess.
f: How does CRUSH choose where data lives?
What are the downsides?
p: Ceph unifies block, object and file storage with replication and CRUSH. Shared RBD pools give instant copy-on-write clones and shared-storage live migration. Cost is operational complexity.
tip: Say shared pools make clone-from-image instant.

q: What are volume types and how do you use them for service tiers?
a: A volume type is a label that maps to a set of extra specs, which tell the scheduler and driver how to place and configure a volume. For example a type called ssd can map to a Ceph pool on NVMe and a type called hdd to a capacity pool, and the extra spec volume_backend_name chooses the back end. You can also attach QoS specs such as maximum IOPS and throughput, encryption settings, replication and multi-attach capability. Types can be public or private to specific projects, which is how you offer premium storage only to some tenants. Users select a type at creation time, and operators can retype existing volumes, with migration if the back end changes. This makes volume types the primary tool for building a storage catalogue with distinct performance, cost and protection levels.
f: How do you restrict a type to one project?
What does retype do when the back end differs?
p: Volume types map to back ends and policies through extra specs and QoS. Use them to offer tiers like ssd and hdd, and to restrict premium types to specific projects.
cmds: openstack volume type create --property volume_backend_name=ceph-nvme fast
openstack volume qos create --consumer front-end --property read_iops_sec=5000 fast-qos
tip: Present types as your storage catalogue.

q: What is boot from volume and what are its advantages?
a: With boot from volume, the instance root disk is a Cinder volume rather than an ephemeral disk on the hypervisor. You create it from an image, and Nova attaches it as the boot device. The big advantages are persistence and mobility. The disk survives instance deletion if you keep the volume, it can be snapshotted and backed up with Cinder tools, and the instance can be evacuated or live-migrated without copying the disk when the storage is shared. It also allows larger root disks than local flavors, and boot is quick with Ceph clones. The downsides are dependence on the storage network and Cinder availability, since a storage outage now means the instances' root disks are unavailable, and slightly more complex quota management for volumes. For production pets and databases I favour boot from volume; for stateless cattle, ephemeral is fine.
f: What is delete_on_termination?
When is ephemeral storage better?
p: The root disk is a Cinder volume, so it persists, can be snapshotted and makes evacuation easy. It depends on the storage backend. Ephemeral still fits stateless instances.
cmds: openstack server create --volume ubuntu-vol --flavor m1.small --network n1 web1
tip: Contrast pets and cattle to justify the choice.

q: How do Cinder snapshots and backups differ?
a: A snapshot is a point-in-time copy kept on the same storage back end, usually implemented as an efficient copy-on-write reference, so it is fast and space cheap but it shares the fate of the storage system. If the Ceph cluster is lost, the snapshots are lost too. A backup is a copy made by the Cinder backup service to a separate target, such as Swift, S3, NFS or another Ceph cluster, optionally incremental, so it protects against back-end failure, accidental deletion and corruption. I use snapshots for quick rollbacks before changes and cloning, and backups for real recovery and retention policies. For consistent backups of databases I quiesce the application or use a crash-consistent approach with a clear understanding of what is guaranteed, and I regularly test restore, because an untested backup is only a hope.
f: What are incremental backups?
How do you get application-consistent snapshots?
p: Snapshots are fast, same-backend point-in-time copies. Backups go to a separate target and survive backend loss. Use both, and test restores.
cmds: openstack volume snapshot create --volume data1 snap1
openstack volume backup create --incremental --name bk2 data1
openstack volume backup restore bk2 data1-restored
tip: One-liner: snapshots share the fate of the backend; backups do not.

q: A volume is stuck in attaching, detaching or error_deleting. How do you recover?
a: First I find out whether the problem is in Nova, Cinder or the storage back end. I check the volume's attachment records in Cinder and the block device mappings in Nova, because most stuck states come from these two disagreeing. I read the cinder-volume and nova-compute logs by request ID, and check whether the connection really exists on the host, using iscsiadm, multipath or rbd status. If the backend operation has completed but the state was not updated, I use the reset-state admin command for the volume or the attachment to move it to a consistent state, and then detach or delete normally. If a back-end volume is truly gone or locked, I fix it on the storage system. I avoid editing the database by hand, and I add an alert on volumes stuck in transitional states longer than a threshold.
f: What does reset-state do?
How do you find orphan attachments?
p: Compare Cinder attachments with Nova block device mappings, read logs by request ID, check the host connection, then use reset-state to align them. Alert on long transitional states.
cmds: openstack volume show data1 -c status -c attachments
tip: Say Nova and Cinder disagreeing is the root of most stuck states.

q: What is multi-attach and when is it safe to use?
a: Multi-attach lets one Cinder volume be attached to more than one instance at the same time. It must be enabled through a volume type with the multiattach property, and the back end must support it. It is not magic shared storage: a normal file system such as ext4 or XFS will be corrupted if two hosts mount it read-write. It is safe only with a cluster-aware file system, like GFS2 or OCFS2, with a cluster manager, or in read-only use cases, for example distributing a shared dataset read-only to many nodes. It is also used for some shared-disk database or clustering software that handles fencing, such as active-passive failover with SCSI reservations. If you need a shared file system for general use, Manila with CephFS or NFS is the right answer, not multi-attach. Finally, I would say how I would document this for the team so the knowledge does not live only in one person's head.
f: Why does ext4 corrupt under multi-attach?
When is Manila the better choice?
p: One volume attached to several instances, via a multiattach volume type. Only safe with cluster-aware filesystems or read-only use; for general shared files use Manila.
cmds: openstack volume type create --property multiattach='<is> True' shared
openstack server add volume node2 shared1
tip: Say clearly that multi-attach does not equal shared filesystem.

q: How does Swift object storage work: rings, replicas and consistency?
a: Swift stores objects, which are files with metadata, in containers under accounts, accessed over HTTP. Proxy servers accept requests and use a ring, a consistent-hashing structure, to determine which storage nodes hold each partition. Objects are replicated, usually three times, across zones, and the account, container and object servers on storage nodes store the data. Swift favours availability and eventual consistency: a write succeeds when a quorum of replicas confirm it, and background replicators and auditors repair missing or corrupted data. Adding capacity means rebalancing the ring, which moves a controlled number of partitions to avoid overload. Swift suits large unstructured data such as backups, media and archives, and it scales out linearly, but it is not a file system and not for low-latency block use. Many clouds now use Ceph RGW instead for S3 compatibility.
f: What is the ring?
Why is rebalancing done gradually?
p: Proxies use a consistent-hashing ring to place replicas across zones; replicators and auditors provide eventual consistency and repair. Scales linearly for object data.
tip: Explain the ring as consistent hashing with zones.

q: What is Manila and how does it differ from Cinder?
a: Manila is the shared file system service. Where Cinder gives a block device that one instance, normally, formats and owns, Manila gives a network file system share, NFS, CIFS or CephFS, that many instances can mount at the same time. A user creates a share of a share type, grants access by IP, user or cephx key, and mounts it from inside the guest. Manila drivers manage back ends, such as CephFS, NetApp, or a generic driver that builds a share from a Cinder volume in a service instance. Use Manila for shared content, home directories, build caches and Kubernetes ReadWriteMany volumes. Because share traffic travels over a network the instance can reach, the network design needs a path from tenant networks to the storage network, and security is handled through access rules. I would also mention the main failure mode and how I would detect it early, since operations experience shows in how you talk about what goes wrong.
f: How do you give a tenant network access to CephFS?
When is Cinder still the better choice?
p: Manila provides shared NFS, CIFS or CephFS file systems with access rules, for many-instance sharing. Cinder gives a private block device per instance.
cmds: openstack share create --share-type cephfs NFS 100 --name data
openstack share access create data ip 10.0.0.0/24
openstack share export location list data
tip: Use ReadWriteMany for Kubernetes as the practical example.

q: How do you size and monitor a Ceph cluster for OpenStack?
a: I size by usable capacity after replication, which for three replicas is one third of raw, and I keep a healthy margin, typically staying below about 70 to 75 percent so recovery after a failure has room. For performance I count OSDs and device types, NVMe for latency sensitive pools and HDD for capacity, since IOPS scale with the number of OSDs. The network matters just as much: a separate cluster network for replication, at least 25 GbE for dense nodes, and no oversubscription. I set failure domains, host or rack, in CRUSH so replicas never share one.
